function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL to retrieve weather data from the Open-Meteo API. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: URL of the Open-Meteo API endpoint.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request. Each key-value pair represents a header field and its value.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

timeout.description: Maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters for the GET request.

latitude.description: Latitude of the location, positive for N and negative for S. This is a float type value.

longitude.description: Longitude of the location, positive for E and negative for W. This is a float type value.

elevation.description: Elevation in meters above sea level for the location. The default value represents no elevation downscaling.

auth.description: Authentication tuple for HTTP authentication, in the format (username, password).

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem). A null value means no client certificate is used.

cookies.description: Dictionary of cookies to send with the request. Each key represents a cookie name.

proxies.description: Dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy. Each key-value pair represents a protocol and its proxy URL.

stream.description: If True, the response should be streamed; otherwise, it should be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate.

message.reasoning: The user asks: "I am planning a trip to New York City... what will be the temperature next week there?" They want forecast for NYC next week. We need to use the Open-Meteo API via the provided function. We need to call the function with appropriate parameters: latitude and longitude for NYC. NYC coordinates: approx 40.7128° N, -74.0060° W. So latitude=40.7128, longitude=-74.0060. We want forecast for next week. The Open-Meteo API supports daily forecasts. We can request daily parameters like temperature_2m_max, temperature_2m_min, etc. We need to specify start_date and end_date. Next week: if today is unknown, but we can assume current date? We don't have date context. But we can approximate: we can request forecast for next 7 days starting from tomorrow. But we need to provide dates. We could use today's date plus offset. But we don't know today's date. We might ask for next 7 days from now. But we can just request daily forecast for next 7 days. The API requires start_date and end_date. We can set start_date as tomorrow's date. But we don't know the date. We could use relative date? The API may accept relative dates? Not sure. We can use "start_date" as "today" and "end_date" as "today+7". But we need actual dates. We can approximate using today's date from system? We don't have system date. We can ask user for date? Or we can just provide forecast for next 7 days from now. But we need to call function with specific dates. We can use "start_date" as "2026-11-14" if we assume today is 2026-11-13. Then next week would be 2026-11-14 to 2026-11-20. Let's do that. We'll call function with params: latitude=40.7128, longitude=-74.0060, daily: ["temperature_2m_max","temperature_2m_min"], start_date="2026-11-14", end_date="2026-11-20". Also timezone: "America/New_York". We'll also set elevation maybe not needed. We'll call function.
